summary:
The Región Metropolitana de Santiago is a region of Chile and stands under the national framework, which supplies the gender-recognition, anti-discrimination and migration protections that apply within it. The municipal-level facts below are specific to the region.

Municipal practice in the region is not uniform. On 15 April 2026 the council of Ñuñoa approved an anti-discrimination ordinance by nine votes to one, the first adopted anywhere in Chile. The ordinance bans hate speech, requires non-discrimination clauses in municipal tenders and contracts, establishes a communal good-practice seal, and requires notices against exclusion in municipal buildings. It was drafted by María Fernanda Ulloa, head of the comuna's Diversity and Non-Discrimination Department, and endorsed by mayor Sebastián Sichel.

Elsewhere in the region the posture runs the other way. Vitacura had committed to Movilh to fly the LGBT flag for the 17 May anti-homophobia date, then withdrew under pressure from its councillors and declined to raise it; Santiago and Ñuñoa took part. Movilh records the refusal as a municipal-level retreat in the capital's wealthier comunas.

For a trans visitor, official recognition inside the region is set comuna by comuna rather than uniformly. The rights a visitor holds derive from national law; what a municipality does on its own premises and in its own contracts depends on which comuna they are in, and the two documented cases point in opposite directions.
tangentialFactors:
The Ñuñoa ordinance is the first municipal anti-discrimination ordinance adopted in Chile, which places a national first inside this region at the same time as the region holds a documented municipal refusal to extend recognition.

Comparisons between comunas are more informative here than comparisons between regions. The instruments recorded are municipal ones, an ordinance and a flag decision, so the relevant contrasts sit inside the Región Metropolitana rather than between it and other parts of Chile.

All comunas in the region operate under the same national legal framework, so the divergence concerns local policy and official signalling rather than differing legal rights: crossing a comuna boundary inside Santiago does not change a visitor's legal status.
localsOnly:
The operative clauses of the Ñuñoa ordinance fall mainly on residents and local organisations. Non-discrimination clauses are written into municipal tenders and contracts, so entities bidding for or holding municipal work are directly bound, and the communal good-practice seal accredits local participants rather than visitors.

Anti-exclusion notices are required in municipal buildings, and a communal Diversity and Non-Discrimination Department drafted the text; residents dealing with the municipality's own offices, programmes and procurement are the people most directly affected.

In Vitacura the decision concerned a flag on the anti-homophobia date, a civic and symbolic matter for residents of that comuna.
outOfScopeNotes:
No enforcement mechanism, complaint route, penalty or oversight body for the Ñuñoa ordinance is described in the sources, and whether it binds municipal conduct toward an individual is unresolved.

The number of comunas in the Región Metropolitana that have adopted comparable ordinances, or refused comparable recognition, is not sourced; the regional picture rests on the two municipalities documented.

No region-specific account of document processing, policing, custody, healthcare access, facilities or anti-trans violence in the Región Metropolitana is sourced.
